title: The Price of Sugar
full_review:
A worthy documentary, Bill Haney's "The Price of Sugar" (Uncommon) recounts the struggle of a Catholic missionary priest, Father Christopher Hartley, to lead Haitian workers laboring in the sugar fields of the Dominican Republic in a crusade for their most basic social and economic rights.

The film -- narrated with quiet authority by Paul Newman --- is thus both the inspiring story of an individual and the history of a mass movement.

Born into the family of a highly successful English businessman and his aristocratic Spanish wife, Christopher Hartley was raised in a cosmopolitan world of wealth and privilege. Yet, as a follower of Blessed Mother Teresa of Calcutta, he long ago left that world behind to serve the "poorest of the poor." In 1997 that commitment brought him to the Dominican Republic, one of the most poverty-stricken nations in the Western Hemisphere.

As impoverished as most Dominicans are, however, they have in their midst a group of people who are even more destitute: immigrant Haitians who live and work on the Dominican's "bateys," or sugar plantations. A barrier of silence has long surrounded these foreign laborers, and the slaverylike conditions in which they are held.

Breaking through that silence, and serving the religious and material needs of the Haitian workers became Father Hartley's life work. But his mission brought him into conflict, not only with the Dominican Republic's sugar industry -- led by the powerful Vicini family -- but with a portion of the Dominican population as well.

Whether motivated by bribes from the sugar interests or by the pervasive Dominican prejudice against Haitians, large numbers of protesters began to call for Father Hartley's expulsion. Some of these demonstrators can be seen in the film, shouting, chanting and uttering barely concealed threats against the priest.

Father Hartley, meanwhile, is shown ministering to the Haitian immigrants, organizing medical visits for them, and encouraging them to stand up, peacefully, for their rights. He stresses their need for unity and courage in the face of intimidation. (Since the film was made, Father Hartley left the Dominican Republic in obedience to his religious superiors and is now ministering in Ethiopia.)

Though Haney's film provides an unsettling look at the conditions under which the Haitians live and work, its message is by no means entirely bleak. This is a tale of exploitation. But it is also, fundamentally, a celebration of the good that can spring from one individual's deep religious commitment and from well-organized, nonviolent methods of mass resistance.

The film contains graphic depictions of disease and brief nudity among bathing children. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-II -- adults and adolescents. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
